cl_fent_fake_pills.q: Are fake pills with fentanyl getting more common?
cl_fent_fake_pills.short: Yes, in US records to 2021. Overdose deaths with signs of fake pills rose from 2 to about 5 in 100, and to about 15 in 100 in western states.
cl_fent_fake_pills.but: Nobody tested what share of street pills hold fentanyl. These are police and death records, and death records likely miss many fake pills.
how: US police records: of seizures that held fentanyl, pills were 14 in 100 in early 2018 and 29 in 100 in late 2021. The rest were powder. Fentanyl pills seized in three months rose from about 42,000 to about 2.1 million.

Death records from 29 states and Washington, DC: deaths with signs of fake pills went from 2 in 100 in mid-2019 to a high of about 5 in 100 in mid-2021, then stayed near there. In western states, about 5 became about 15 in 100.

In 2021, 55 in 100 of these deaths involved fake oxycodone only, often marked 'M-30', and 17 in 100 fake alprazolam (Xanax) only. Fentanyl or similar drugs were among the recorded causes in 93 in 100.
Neither record shows what the pills held: police data have no pill contents, and death records don't say how many pills were tested. A drug-checking study in Vancouver tested too few pills to say.
cl_fent_fake_pills.rate: Big US record sets. But seizures depend on what police target and test, death records likely miss fake pills, more in some places than others, and nobody tested a fair sample of pills.

cl_opi_overdose_recognition.q: Would I know if someone was overdosing on opioids?
cl_opi_overdose_recognition.short: Not always. On a written test, people trained by overdose programmes spotted about 7 of 9 opioid overdoses. People without that training spotted about 5 of 9.
cl_opi_overdose_recognition.but: It was a paper test with 62 people that staff picked, not real overdoses. Nobody was tested before training, so training may not be the reason.
how: In 2005 and 2006, 62 people at six US overdose programmes read 16 short stories. Each was based on what someone who injects drugs had called an overdose. Medical experts had decided 9 were opioid overdoses needing naloxone, and 7 were not.
Trained people spotted about 7 of the 9 opioid overdoses, untrained people about 5. Trained people still didn't choose naloxone in about 2 of the 9; untrained people missed about 3.
Both groups got only about 4 or 5 of the other 7 stories right. Even the experts said there wasn't enough information in about a quarter of their answers.
The paper doesn't say which stories people got wrong. So it can't show which signs get missed, or whether people can tell a heavy nod from an overdose.
cl_opi_overdose_recognition.rate: One small study. Staff picked who took part, nobody was tested before training, and it used written stories, not real overdoses. It doesn't say which stories people got wrong.

cl_mdma_pill_content.q: Is ecstasy really MDMA, and how strong are the pills?
cl_mdma_pill_content.short: Often, but not always. In European pill tests in 2009, 19 to 64 in 100 pills held MDMA, depending on the country. By 2013 most did, and held more of it.
cl_mdma_pill_content.but: These were pills people chose to bring in, and the newest tests are from 2013. Pills today may be different.
how: A 2004 review of pill tests found MDMA in 90 to 98 in 100 ecstasy pills from the 1980s to the early 1990s, 50 to 80 in 100 in the mid-1990s, and nearly all by the early 2000s. Others held related drugs, other things such as ketamine or caffeine, or nothing active.

Drug-checking services in five European countries tested pills people brought in, from 2008 to 2013. Pills holding MDMA dropped in 2009, to about 19 in 100 in Austria and 64 in 100 in the Netherlands, then mostly recovered. Newer drugs such as mCPP or PMMA turned up in some ecstasy.

The MDMA in a pill ranged from none to about 150 mg in older tests. Where measured, the average rose from about 61 to 74 mg in 2009 to about 103 to 114 mg in 2013: nearly double in the Netherlands, less elsewhere. These are lab measurements, not amounts to take.

Some people feel little from a pill, and some then take more. A weaker pill, or one with no MDMA, is one possible reason; in an Australian survey, people thought about 1 pill in 4 or 5 was a dud. Neither source looked at other reasons, such as tolerance, or at what happens when people then take more.
cl_mdma_pill_content.rate: Lab tests of pills people chose to hand in, dropped in bins or police seized, so not a fair picture of all pills sold. Labs used different methods, and the newest data are from 2013.

fentanyl-and-analogues.statement: By late 2021, about 15 in 100 overdose deaths in the western US showed signs of fake pills.
fentanyl-and-analogues.why: That was up from about 5 in 100 in mid-2019. Death records likely miss many fake pills, so the true share may be higher.

prescription-opioids.statement: In US overdose deaths with signs of fake pills, most fakes copied oxycodone.
prescription-opioids.why: In 2021 records, 55 in 100 of these deaths involved fake oxycodone only, often marked 'M-30'. Death records likely miss many fake pills.

heroin.statement: Even experts often said a short overdose story did not tell them enough.
heroin.why: They said so in about a quarter of their answers. It was one small US study, using written stories, not real overdoses.

heroin.statement: Trained people spotted every opioid overdose on a paper test.
heroin.why: They spotted about 7 of 9, against about 5 of 9 for people without training. It was a paper test with 62 people that staff picked.

mdma.statement: Pills sold as ecstasy have nearly always held MDMA.
mdma.why: In European tests in 2009, as few as 19 in 100 pills held MDMA in one country. These were pills people chose to bring in.
